items.description: Glasslake Funding’s Doug Robinson: FINTRAC non-compliance is a risk brokers can no longer ignore
items.content: <p>Glasslake Funding’s Doug Robinson: FINTRAC non-compliance is a risk brokers can no longer ignore</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282884379552081.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Glasslake Funding’s Doug Robinson: FINTRAC non-compliance is a risk brokers can no longer ignore
items.body:
With additional reporting by Fergal McAlinden

Two years after mortgage brokers became reporting entities under Canada’s anti-money laundering framework, a senior industry voice is sounding a warning: the window for wilful inaction has closed.

Doug Robinson of Glasslake Funding, a Toronto-based alternative mortgage lender, drew on a dual background in policing and lending to take stock of where brokerages stand on compliance.

Robinson was speaking at the Mortgage Professionals Canada conference in Calgary, two years on from October 11, 2024, the date on which the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) brought mortgage administrators, brokers and lenders under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA).

“I can pretty much guarantee this will not blow over,” Robinson said.

“If you’re a broker or owning a brokerage and you haven’t done any work on FINTRAC stuff, you may want to.”

Robinson described two camps that emerged when the rules were first announced: those who hired compliance staff, documented policies and prepared in earnest, and those who hoped the requirements might quietly disappear.

As the debate over challenging FINTRAC requirements for brokers rumbles into 2026, Robinson argued the regulator’s baseline expectations are more achievable than commonly assumed.

“FINTRAC doesn’t want mortgage brokers to become experts in reporting money launderers,” he said.

“They just wanted to add mortgage brokers because you guys are governed by a regulator and you have an obligation, and it fortifies Canada’s anti-money laundering landscape.”

Know your client — or know the risk

Robinson anchored his anti-money laundering (AML) framework around three questions every broker must be able to answer: who is the applicant, how will they service the mortgage, and where did the down payment come from? The third, he said, is the most exploited vulnerability in the transaction chain.

“In lending and in mortgages, the down payment is usually, in my opinion, the softest spot,” Robinson said.

“If someone’s looking to get a whole bunch of money into the system in one spot, they’ll usually do it through down payment.”

He urged brokers to build what he called “reasonability statements” — documented explanations that account for the origin of funds — warning that gift letters alone carry limited evidentiary weight.

“The reasonability statements go a long way,” he said. 

Policies, risk ratings, and a lender blind spot

Robinson outlined five elements every brokerage should have in place:

  1. a designated compliance officer or administrator
  2. written policies
  3. a company-level risk assessment
  4. AML training — leverageable through MPC for smaller shops
  5. a completed two-year self-assessment

 A smaller brokerage, he noted, can assign compliance responsibilities to an administrative staff member, provided the function is kept separate from the sales side.

His sharpest criticism was aimed at lenders. “In my opinion, lenders are soft on being concerned about where the repayment comes from,” Robinson said.

Accelerated or lump-sum payments made after funding, he argued, too often pass without scrutiny, a gap that sophisticated money laundering schemes are positioned to exploit.

Robinson also flagged British Columbia’s unexplained wealth orders (UWOs), a civil mechanism under the province’s Civil Forfeiture Act that can compel individuals to account for assets exceeding $75,000 that appear disproportionate to their known income, all without requiring a criminal conviction.

Some mortgage professionals argue that regulation is both burdensome and necessary. Robinson, a former police officer, sits firmly in the latter camp. He suggested the UWO model could spread beyond British Columbia as the courts test its constitutional limits.

“There’s no downside to reporting an unusual transaction report to FINTRAC,” he said.

“Sometimes big investigations start from a really small report that someone put in sometime.”

items._ogDesc: GTA new home sales rose in September but remain historically weak. Single-family prices plunged $180k in four months, while condo sales hit a record low.
items.body:
Greater Toronto Area (GTA) new home sales picked up in September, but the recovery remains shaky. BILD and Altus Group data shows sales rose 63.9% from last year, but they remain historically weak. The bigger story is prices—nearly a third of the single-family correction has occurred in the past 4 months. New condo prices have held up better, but buyers are balking with sales hitting a record low for the segment.

Toronto New Single-Family Homes Fell $180k In The Past 4 Months

The Altus Group benchmark price of single-family and condo apartment homes across Greater Toronto.

Source: Altus Group; BILD GTA.

New home prices continued to slide, led by single-family homes. The segment’s benchmark slipped 0.2% (-$2.1k) to $1.25 million in September, down 13.3% (-$190.7k) from last year. September’s decline was modest, but the bigger story is the sudden return of plunging prices.

Prices have effectively fallen off a cliff since May, dropping 12.7% (-$180.8k) in just four months. That accounts for nearly 95% of the decline over the past year. The benchmark is now 35.5% (-$687.1k) below its July 2022 record high. The percentage decline over the past four months alone is more than a third of the total decline from the peak, leaving prices where they were almost 6 years ago.

New condo prices have held up much better. The segment’s benchmark fell 1.0% (-$10.3k) to $1.03 million in September, just 0.2% (-$1.7k) below last year. Prices are now 17.6% (-$220.9k) below the March 2022 record high—roughly half the percentage decline seen in single-family homes. That relative strength has narrowed the price gap between the two segments to just $215.2k. Whether that means single-family homes are now relatively weak or new condos are set to correct further is anyone’s guess. However, a breakdown of home sales suggests demand for new condos at these prices is almost non-existent.

New Home Sales Rise, But New Condo Sales Hit A September Low

Greater Toronto new home sales in September.

Source: Altus Group; BildGTA; Better Dwelling.

New home sales jumped, but the above chart should temper expectations. There were 949 units sold in September, up 63.9% from last year. Single-family homes accounted for 820 sales, the strongest September since 2021. Condos weren’t so lucky: just 129 units sold, down 40.3% from last year and the weakest September on record.

The increase is welcome, but a base effect makes it sound more impressive than reality. Despite the jump, total sales remained 52% below the 10-year September average. Sales of single-family homes have recovered, while condo demand continues to find new lows.

New Home Inventory Falls, But Remains Elevated

New home inventory fell but remains lofty by the region’s historical standards. There were 19,957 new homes for sale in September, down 8.2% from last year. Despite falling below the past two years, inventory remains at its third-highest September level since 2015. New home inventory might be lighter, but relative to sales, this remains a weak demand balance.

Toronto’s new home sales improved, but the numbers are less impressive when broken down. Single-family sales picked up alongside steep declines in prices. As for condos, prices are firmer, but with sales at record lows, buyers are balking at those prices. Last month’s numbers are even less impressive when one considers it’s the result of billions in bailout programs. From developer bailouts to tax incentives, that’s a lot of public support for a market struggling to find buyers.

items.title: Slower homebuilding risks wiping out Canada’s affordability gains, economists warn
items.description: The national housing market may be sluggish, but the lacklustre pace of housing construction could worsen affordability problems
items.content: <p>The national housing market may be sluggish, but the lacklustre pace of housing construction could worsen affordability problems</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639282861144967017.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The national housing market may be sluggish, but the lacklustre pace of housing construction could worsen affordability problems
items.body:
Canada’s housing market has been mired in a years-long slump, pushing prices lower amid plunging demand – but economists still say the sluggish pace of homebuilding could worsen the affordability crisis in the long run.

Mathieu Laberge (pictured top), chief economist and senior vice president at Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) and Stéfane Marion, chief economist and strategist at National Bank of Canada, sounded an ominous note on the construction outlook during speeches at the recent Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) National conference in Calgary.

Laberge highlighted how the slower pace of construction in 2026 could have significant negative consequences for the market down the line.

“Our latest housing supply report points to the central issue: right here, right now across Canada, construction is slowing faster than the underlying need for housing,” he said. “If we react to a softer market by stopping too much construction, we may be protecting ourselves from today’s risks – but we’re also creating tomorrow’s shortages.

“We are at a very high risk that by not providing the appropriate and sufficient supply today, we will lose the improvement in affordability we’ve seen two or three, or five years down the road.”

Residential construction continues to slide

The Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) recently revised its home price growth forecast downward for the year, basing that adjustment on waning purchase demand because of wider economic uncertainty and rising interest rates.

Construction in certain sectors is grinding to a halt against that backdrop. Marion noted that a sizable portion of recently-built condos has not been absorbed, marking the highest proportion seen since the early 1990s – and the resulting homebuilding slowdown has been stark.

Laberge said just six companies of more than 500 employees currently build residential homes across the country, and the sector is also being left behind in the new digital era. In a recent McKinsey study of the level of digitization across industries, construction came second last, he pointed out – only ahead of hunting and agriculture.

Canada building the wrong home types, says Laberge

It’s also often pointed out that the type of home construction currently being prioritized is missing the mark. Condominium construction, particularly in Toronto and Vancouver, has dominated homebuilding in recent decades – leaving a surplus of smaller condos rather than family-sized homes.

“Canada doesn’t simply have too much or too little housing,” Laberge said. “The reality is that we have a mismatch between the homes people need and the homes the system is producing. What’s small is unaffordable and what’s large is unavailable.

“This is the supply families need and they are seeking desperately, and they cannot find it right now.”

What’s more, the homebuying lull isn’t destined to last forever, and a ramping-up of purchase activity could put even further strain on national housing supply if construction doesn’t gather pace.

“It takes, give or take, six to eight years to deliver a big housing unit, whether it’s condo or rental, in any of the larger centres across Canada. Demand can shift on a dime,” Laberge cautioned.

“Young adults living with parents, people sharing homes longer than they plan, newcomers settling permanently, and families delaying their next move can all come back into the market when confidence returns. And that will return at some point. This is not a one-year story. This is a pent-up demand story that will play out over the next three, four, five years.”

For now, there seems little prospect of homebuilding accelerating to meet the required annual level – particularly with more than a million extra workers in the construction industry needed, according to Marion, to satisfy demand.

Laberge said it makes no sense to ease off on construction even in a quieter market because it will ultimately have a negative effect on the affordability outlook. “We should not close a fire station because it’s raining,” he said. “We should welcome the rain but not sell the truck.”

items.title: Larger GTA condos defy correction as one-bedrooms slide further
items.description: New Wahi analysis finds four-bedroom GTA condos up while studio sales nearly vanish
items.content: <p>New Wahi analysis finds four-bedroom GTA condos up while studio sales nearly vanish</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282832912037174.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: New Wahi analysis finds four-bedroom GTA condos up while studio sales nearly vanish
items.body:
The Greater Toronto Area’s condominium market is fracturing along size lines. New research from Wahi, a Toronto-based digital real estate platform and brokerage, finds that buyers who acquired larger units at the outset of the pandemic are still holding gains, while the one-bedroom segment has dropped 14% from Q1 2020 and has recorded flat or negative pricing in every consecutive quarter since Q1 2022.

The analysis compares median sale prices and transaction volumes across condominium types between Q1 2020 and Q1 2026, adding texture to a correction that Canadian mortgage professionals have followed closely.

Wahi’s tracking of GTA days on market through the first half of 2026 showed condominiums averaging 36 days to find a buyer in Q2 2026, roughly three to four times longer than during the market’s 2022 peak. 

Small units feel the weight of investor retreat

The data is most acute at the bottom of the size ladder. In Q1, the median price of a one-bedroom Greater Toronto Area condominium was $480,000, with 1,574 units changing hands. That's down 39% from Q1 2020 and 66% below the peak recorded in Q1 2021.

Studios have fared even worse. Just seven transactions were recorded in the first quarter of 2026, against a high of 230 in Q1 2022.

“In today’s GTA condo market, the end user is the main source of anything resembling demand,” said Ryan McLaughlin, economist at Wahi.

“There simply isn’t much appetite among buyers for smaller units, which have historically been geared primarily towards investors looking to flip them and/or rent them out.”

The broker community has had a front-row seat to the fallout. Christine Xu, founder of Money Broker Canada and a 26-year industry veteran, described the pre-construction investor collapse starkly when speaking at MortgageFest Canada 2026.

“A lot of those people are racing masters — they invest in a whole bunch of pre-construction condos and they are being hit the most. Big shot realtors who bought so many pre-construction condos and now — bankruptcy. We see bankruptcy all over the place,” she said.

On pricing, Xu was equally direct: “The price is almost 50% of the original purchase price. So the original owner walked away, gave the condo back to the builder.”

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada, says Ottawa should allow foreign buyers to purchase new-build homes, pointing to unsold condo inventory and the government's goal of making Canada more attractive to investors. https://t.co/hUVWtFthRu — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 20, 2026

Larger units offer a buffer — for now

Further up the size spectrum, the picture is more resilient, though still far from comfortable. Two-bedroom condominiums recorded a Q1 2026 median of $630,000, just 2% above Q1 2020 levels.

Three-bedroom units reached $700,000 — a 13% gain — while four-plus-bedroom condos led all categories at $715,000, up 15% over the six-year study period.

Transaction volumes have not been spared regardless of size: two-bedroom sales fell 35% from Q1 2020, three-bedroom activity dropped 43%, and four-plus-bedroom transactions declined 33%.

“Although this is likely not the kind of appreciation condo owners are hoping for, these numbers demonstrate something important about the GTA real estate market in general,” McLaughlin said.

“Even in the harshest environment in decades, buyers who purchase the right type of unit and are able to hold on for the longer term are insulated from the worst effects of a correction.”

“What’s striking is these units have maintained pricing even as sales volumes have collapsed across the board,” he added.

“However, it seems that buyers of larger three- and four-bedroom units have less room for price negotiation.”

For end users — the segment McLaughlin identifies as the market’s only real source of demand — the window may be more open than headlines suggest.

Reaza Ali, national business development manager at Heartwood Financial Group, told MortgageFest Canada 2026, “The market has come into a position now, that those with resources, it’s a fantastic opportunity to jump in... I would focus in on is the affordability piece there, because the price points on these properties are more in line with where they should have been.”

items.description: Tru Cooperative Bank CEO says proportionate rules are key to boosting banking competition in Canada
items.content: <p>Tru Cooperative Bank CEO says proportionate rules are key to boosting banking competition in Canada</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282819062614560.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tru Cooperative Bank CEO says proportionate rules are key to boosting banking competition in Canada
items.body:
Canada’s newest federal credit union is calling on Ottawa to overhaul its merger and regulatory framework, warning that without meaningful reform, smaller institutions cannot build national scale and Canadians will be left with a banking market dominated by a handful of major lenders.

In an opinion piece published in The Hill Times, Launi Skinner, CEO of Tru Cooperative Bank in Langley, British Columbia, outlined three priorities for the federal government:

  1. clearer merger regulations and appropriate tax treatment
  2. coordinated review processes across federal agencies
  3. capital requirements calibrated to an institution’s actual size and risk profile

“For far too long, Canadians have had limited choice when it comes to national banking options,” Skinner wrote.

Tru Cooperative Bank, formerly First West Credit Union, became federally regulated in April and currently serves approximately 290,000 members with approximately $21 billion in total assets and assets under administration.

In September, it announced a proposed merger with Ontario’s Libro Credit Union that would create an organization serving approximately 470,000 members with nearly $33 billion in combined assets, subject to member and regulatory approvals.

The case for a stronger middle tier

Canada’s national residential mortgage market carries more than $2.4 trillion in outstanding debt, according to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) data for December 2025, yet most credit unions remain regionally concentrated.

“Canada needs more institutions between those two ends of the market,” Skinner wrote — cooperatives with national capabilities and the local accountability that distinguishes them from publicly traded banks.

The appetite to fill that gap is already visible at the lender level. At MortgageFest Canada 2026, Bekim Merdita, head of sales and marketing at QuestBank, formerly Community Trust, described the institution’s positioning. 

“Community Trust, 50-year-old trust company. And really, at the end of last year, we got our banking licence — a Schedule 1 bank — and rebranded ourselves to Quest Bank. It gives us the ability to not just do mortgage products, but other products as well that serve the consumer and really start building a financial ecosystem for our consumer.”

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) has signalled a less conservative approach to approving new banking entrants, and the regulator’s updated approvals framework launched in June aims to widen market access further.

For brokers navigating a more complex lender roster, regulatory inconsistency is already a top frustration. Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer of WealthOne Bank of Canada, told MortgageFest Canada 2026. 

"The biggest pain points that we’re hearing from brokers is the ever-changing policies, the ever-changing rules, the ever-changing processes that lenders are doing," he said. 

"Every single week a lender has changed how you submit a deal, what forms you need, what documents — and brokers are struggling to keep up."

What Ottawa needs to do

Skinner argued that mergers involving federal credit unions — requiring review by OSFI, the Competition Bureau, and the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC), alongside the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC) and the Department of Finance — should not generate duplicative information requests or conflicting regulatory interpretations.

“No responsible cooperative leader is asking for weaker consumer protection or lower standards of safety and soundness,” she wrote.

“But equivalent standards do not always require identical requirements.”

She also called for proportionate capital rules, arguing requirements designed around systemically important banks divert management capacity away from cybersecurity, digital banking, and small-business lending at mid-sized cooperatives.

Federally regulated credit unions now hold approximately $47 billion of the $330 billion in total assets across Canadian credit unions nationally, according to the Canadian Credit Union Association (CCUA).

The Tru–Libro combination, if approved, would represent the sector’s most substantial attempt yet to fill the gap Skinner has identified, and the clearest test of whether Ottawa’s updated framework can deliver.

items.title: Amazon-Leased Ajax Facility Listed As Part Of 3-Building Industrial Portfolio
items.description:
Markets speak, and the commercial real estate market in the Greater Toronto Area is indicating that there is a demand for institutional-grade industrial properties, according to yet another new listing for a high-profile industrial property that came online this week.

After a TELUS-leased industrial property and a Tesla-leased industrial property were listed in recent weeks, this time around it is an industrial property leased to Amazon, among others.

The property is an industrial park consisting of three buildings located at 789 Salem Road North, 689 Salem Road North, and 210 Kerrison Drive East in Ajax. The three properties span a total of 107 acres along Salem Road North between Rossland Road East and Kerrison Drive East.

789 Salem Road North spans 58.2 acres, was constructed in 2021, and is home to 1,080,710 sq. ft of space that is 100% leased to tech giant Amazon.

689 Salem Road North spans 9.7 acres, was constructed in 2023, and is home to 181,281 sq. ft of space that is 100% leased to wholesale company All-Special and panel manufacturer SkyRise Prefab Building Solutions.

Lastly, 210 Kerrison Drive East spans 39.1 acres, was constructed in 2022, and is home to 716,548 sq. ft of space that is 100% leased to clothing company H&M.

The properties are owned by CPSP Ajax Nominee Inc. — a joint venture between investment firm Crestpoint Real Estate Investments and pension fund PSP Investments — and belong to the GTA East Industrial Park originally developed by Crestpoint, Broccolini, and Blackwood Partners.

The Listing

Earlier this month, 789 Salem Road North, 689 Salem Road North, and 210 Kerrison Drive East were together listed for sale by Reid Taylor, Lucas Atkins, Matthew Thrift, Connor Molony, Graham Meader, Colin Alves, Luke Dawson, and Edward Plumley of Colliers on an unpriced basis.

  • Address: 789 Salem Road North, 689 Salem Road North, and 210 Kerrison Drive East, Ajax
  • Year Built: 2021 / 2023 / 2022
  • Site Area: 107.0 acres
  • Gross Leasable Area: 1,978,539 sq. ft
  • Current Occupancy Rate: 100%
  • Price: Unpriced
  • Listed By: Colliers (Reid Taylor, Lucas Atkins, Matthew Thrift, Connor Molony, Graham Meader, Colin Alves, Luke Dawson, and Edward Plumley)

According to Colliers, the buildings are equipped with “state-of-the-art” shipping and receiving infrastructure, 40-ft clear heights, and large-format functional warehouse configurations. The properties also include a total of 227 truck-level shipping doors, 363 trailer parking stalls, and 1,160 dedicated vehicle stalls.

The tenancies have a weighted average lease term of 6.8 years, and Colliers says the tenants have made significant capital investments in their spaces. Amazon’s facility was purpose-built for them, H&M’s facility includes an automated conveyor system, and All-Special’s space includes modular cold storage installations.

“At 1.98 million sf, the Portfolio represents approximately 4% of GTA East’s total industrial inventory,” said Colliers in a listing brochure obtained by STOREYS. “Limited near-term power availability in Durham Region makes future development in the immediate area challenging, rendering this scale of product difficult to replicate. The Portfolio is well-positioned to capitalize on sustained demand within Canada’s most critical and supply-constrained industrial market.”

There’s also the location, which is approximately 2 km from Highway 401, provides access to Highway 407 and 412, and is within a 35-minute drive of downtown Toronto. The assets also benefit from the state of the industrial market.

“Greater Toronto is one of North America’s top-performing industrial markets, with a current vacancy rate of 2.2%,” added Colliers. “Demand is supported by a growing consumer base and continued investment in domestic supply chains, while land scarcity and elevated development costs constrain new supply. This offering provides global investors with a valuable long-term land position and immediate scale in one of Canada’s most sought-after industrial markets.”

items.title: GTA High-Rise Sales Sink To A September Record Low
items.description:
Builders in the Greater Toronto Area sold 820 new low-rise homes in September, 17% above the 10-year average for the month. It’s the sixth month in a row low-rise sales have cleared that bar, which covers every month since the HST rebate program launched.

High-rise went the other way. Just 129 new high-rise units sold in September, according to new figures from the Building Industry and Land Development Association (BILD) and Altus Group, BILD’s official source for new home market data. That’s the lowest September on record for the segment, down 40% from September 2025 and 90% below the 10-year average. (BILD’s high-rise category includes units in low-, medium- and high-rise buildings, plus stacked townhouses.)

The low-rise surge isn’t enough to carry the market on its own. Total new home sales came to 949 in September. That’s up significantly from a year ago, and still 52% below the 10-year average of 1,978 units for the month.

Both segments are operating under the same program. BILD and Altus point to its rules around construction start and completion dates as the main obstacle keeping high-rise from taking part the way low-rise has. Altus also names a second problem.

“The high-rise sector remained plagued by undesirable inventory and program constraints centred on unattainable construction timelines,” said Edward Jegg, Research Manager at Altus Group.

High-rise inventory inched up to 12,909 units in September, or roughly 49 months of supply based on average sales over the last 12 months. Low-rise inventory sits at 7,048 homes, or 11 months’ worth.

And within low-rise, buyers are reaching for different product types than they used to.

“In the low-rise market, we have seen a positive response to the HST rebate program with increased sales activity and greater interest in semi-detached homes and townhouses,” said Justin Sherwood, Chief Operating Officer at BILD. “More than half of September’s sales were in semis and townhomes, representing a shift from traditional levels.”

Pricing has moved on that side of the market, too. The benchmark price for a new low-rise home was $1,246,764 in September, down 13.3% over the last 12 months. The high-rise benchmark held at $1,031,574, unchanged from a year ago. Both are gross prices that don’t reflect the HST rebate, so buyers who qualify would see an additional benefit.

Sherwood said the September high-rise numbers show the program rules need to change.

“The high-rise sales performance in September should be a wake-up call that there needs to be further measures and a modification of the program rules to allow the high-rise sector to better participate in the program, which would enable homebuyers in every segment of the housing market to benefit,” he said.

In Simcoe County, the split was starker still: 73 new low-rise homes sold in September at a weighted average price of $998,787, and not a single high-rise unit.

items.description:

The post Canadian Real Estate Needs More Immigration, Foreign Buyers: National Bank appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: National Bank warns Canada’s housing market needs higher immigration and foreign buyers to clear a record inventory of unsold homes and avoid a demographic cliff.
items.body:
Canadian real estate remains out of reach for young adults, but the show must go on. That’s the takeaway from a new housing report from National Bank of Canada. Slow home sales have led to a backlog of developer inventory, but billions in public bailouts are being used to support prices. National Bank urges policymakers to increase their immigration targets and reintroduce foreign buyers to help developers reduce inventory.

Canadian Real Estate In A Slump Despite Billions In Bailouts

The Great Canadian Real Estate Slump isn’t exactly news, but not everyone may be aware of how slow it’s been. Over 1 in 4 (28%) newly completed homes remain unsold, charting new territory for excess supply. “The inventory of completed and unsold housing units across all census metropolitan areas stands at 20,700 units, its highest level since records began in 1990,” warns the bank.

Existing homes aren’t doing much better. Seasonally adjusted sales saw a monthly drop of 2.3% in September, sliding 13% below the 10-year average. While Canadian home prices are now in the biggest correction on record, the almost 5-year slump only rolled back 13 months of price gains. That’s with taxpayer-backed bailouts.

“This demonstrates that the market is so weak that it requires public support,” writes National Bank.

Policymakers aren’t dabbling in support either—they’re fully immersed in the practice. The bank cites Ontario’s $1.3 billion bailout to help investors buy 2,200 unsold Toronto condos. They also cite Ottawa and British Columbia’s $1.45 billion program for roughly the same number of condos. These programs are massive, but even taxpayer-funded bulk buying isn’t enough to clear the backlog.

The bank urges policymakers to drum up more demand. Not from the young adults struggling with shelter costs. They can’t afford to buy a home. They’re calling on Ottawa to look beyond its borders to support prices. Seriously.

Big Six Bank Calls For Higher Immigration To Improve Demand

Canadian real estate prices surged from 2020 and finally peaked in March 2022. That occurred during the pandemic’s population slump, when population growth plummeted to near historic lows. Canada ramped up immigration to unprecedented levels as the slump kicked off. Despite a timing mismatch, reduced immigration is often cited as extending the downturn. The narrative was reinforced by StatCan’s population estimates that revealed a historic contraction. However, that contraction also didn’t happen.

The agency’s recent revisions show the 0.5% y/y decline reported at the start of 2026 was actually 0.5% growth. Ottawa’s plan to reduce non-permanent residents (NPR) to 5% of the population by 2027 is also unlikely. Not only did policymakers delay the target by a year, but NPRs currently represent 6.7% of the population. Canada needs to lose roughly 750,000 NPRs by the end of next year to make those numbers work. Still, the Big Six Bank is concerned.

Reducing NPRs to 5% of the total population will slow total growth to 0.2% in 2027 and 0.1% in 2028, notes the bank. They warn that sticking to the target will mean more downward pressure on housing. “In that context, we believe Ottawa should recalibrate its immigration policy through a targeted and gradual increase in immigration levels,” says National Bank.

Canadians Can’t Afford Homes? Sell Them To Foreign Investors

Canada’s foreign homebuyer restrictions are set to expire in a few months. “The ban on foreign home purchases, which expires on January 1, 2027, should not be extended but rather replaced by a more flexible policy,” explains National Bank.

Whether Canada will renew the moratorium is unclear, but policymakers aren’t fond of the measures. They began to quietly ease foreign buyer restrictions just 86 days after boasting of passing the ban. Canada has since elected Prime Minister Mark Carney, and while he hasn’t addressed the ban directly, the bank notes he recently laid the groundwork for a “controlled increase” in the population.

One of his key fundraisers in BC has been a little more vocal about foreign capital returning to housing. Shortly after PM Carney was elected, Vancouver’s “condo king” said he was working with the PM to drum up foreign capital for rentals.

National Bank sees foreign buyers as one of the only ways developers can sell the homes they built. “We believe it should not be renewed in its current form and that a more flexible model—such as Australia’s, which notably allows foreign buyers to purchase new homes—would help reduce the inventory of unsold housing,” argues the bank.

The bank’s take seems tone-deaf, but the implications are more disturbing. RBC recently found the average first-time buyer plans to buy at 41, 12 years later than current owners did. Separately, they found parents are increasingly helping their adult kids pay bills—a trend most parents attribute to a soaring cost of living rather than poor money management.

Canada’s young adults have been locked out of the housing market. For years they were told that more supply would close the gap, and building more would finally bring prices down. After taxpayers footed the bill to accelerate construction, the narrative abruptly shifted: prices can’t fall further because developers can’t make the math work. Since young adults can’t afford these prices, we suddenly need more temporary residents to support attractive rents that developers can pitch to foreign landlords.

items.content: <p>Desjardins sees Ontario buyers returning, but a Bank of Canada rate jump could cut the recovery short</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639282053551425211.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Desjardins sees Ontario buyers returning, but a Bank of Canada rate jump could cut the recovery short
items.body:
Ontario’s housing market is set for a modest recovery in 2027, with Desjardins Group forecasting a near-5% rise in existing home sales. However, a looming Bank of Canada rate increase could erode the affordability gains brokers are only starting to see.

In its Ontario Housing Outlook, Desjardins senior economist Kari Norman projects provincial resales will reach about 167,000 units next year, up 4.7%, while the average price edges up 2.4% to roughly $825,000.

Lower prices, rising incomes, first-time buyer supports and pent-up demand should pull buyers back, though activity will stay well below long-term norms.

What a Bank of Canada hike would mean for Ontario borrowers

Desjardins expects two quarter-point increases, starting in late October. The central bank has held its overnight rate at 2.25% since October 2025, and its next decision lands October 28 as markets price in a growing likelihood of Bank of Canada rate hikes.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, saw the same signals at MortgageFest 2026.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points,” he said.

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada in Montréal, is less convinced. “I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive,” he told the Mortgage Professionals Canada conference in Calgary, where he also urged brokers to steer clients toward the five-year fixed mortgage.

Daren King of National Bank of Canada and Penelope Graham of Ratehub .ca say five-year fixed-rate mortgages have fallen to a record-low share of new lending as more borrowers opt for variable-rate and shorter-term products. https://t.co/CVKUTrrUL5 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 13, 2026

First-time buyers step into the gap

Toronto’s condo slump remains the biggest drag. Only 525 condo units were started in the City of Toronto in the first nine months of 2026, against nearly 14,000 a year over the previous decade, the report said – a collapse that has left many presale condo buyers facing appraisal shortfalls and lost deposits.

Temporary HST relief of up to $130,000 and Toronto development-charge cuts of 40% to 60% through August 2029 aim to restart activity.

For end users, the reset is an opening. “For people who actually need to buy real estate for their own use, I think that’s really the best time to get into the market,” Christine Xu, founder of Money Broker Canada, said at MortgageFest.

Sarita Free, a mortgage agent with Mortgage Powered Financial Group in Norfolk County, Ontario, sees the same shift.

“With the 30-year amortization that we can now go to, I find a lot of my buyers that have been on the sidelines are finally able to break into the market and stay in their hometown,” she said.

Desjardins projects housing starts will rise about 6% to nearly 65,000 units in 2027, still more than 30% below 2021 and 2022 levels. Norman flagged Canada-US trade tensions and Middle East-driven oil prices as key risks.

items.title: Province pays private developers a premium to acquire key sites
items.description: Specific requirements often push governments to overvalue real estate
items._ogDesc: Specific requirements often push governments to overvalue real estate
items.body:
How much should governments pay to acquire land?

Under the BC NDP, the province has acquired several private properties for public use, paying what some industry sources describe as an unusual premium.

In fall 2025, the province announced that it had allocated $26 million to the Conseil scolaire francophone de la Colombie-Britannique to acquire 3044 Pratt St., Abbotsford, for a Francophone school. Provincial transaction data records a purchase price from a subsidiary of Abbotsford’s Azure Properties Group of $24.6 million, or $2 million an acre (leaving $1.4 million to cover transaction and closing costs).

On Jan. 29, the province acquired a 40-acre property at 1320 McKenzie Rd., Abbotsford, from a subsidiary of Richmond’s Panatch Group for $27.8 million, or $695,000 an acre. The property was used to grow vegetables, but Infrastructure BC plans to build a new Plant and Animal Health Centre on the site in partnership with the B.C. Ministry of Agriculture and Food.

On March 31, Crown corporation BC Hydro acquired a 21.75-acre parcel of vacant industrial land at 2161 Caribou Drive, Langford, from Vancouver-based developers Strand and Bastion Development Corp. for $52.5 million, or an average of $2.4 million an acre.

Howard Chai, who broke news of the deal at The Realist, noted that the “very specific” real estate needs of public entities often result in them appearing to pay more for sites than what other, less constrained parties might.

In the case of the school site in Abbotsford, industry sources indicate that the price was well above not just the $9.8 million value the BC Assessment assigned it on July 1, 2025, but also previous offers by private developers.

One well-known Vancouver developer who spoke to Western Investor on condition of anonymity, considered acquiring the property after it returned to market in fall 2022. Plans filed with the city at the time called for 130 townhomes on a developable area of seven acres. Pricing guidance stood at $24 million.

However, the site’s challenging topography, marked by steep slopes and fish-bearing streams, left just 3.5 acres suitable for development in the view of the developer. It couldn’t justify a price greater than $10 million.

An accepted offer in the range of $18 million ultimately came through, but during the due diligence process the purchaser reduced the offer to $15.5 million—again, because of site considerations. The deal collapsed.

An industry source familiar with the details—also speaking anonymously—called the price the province paid “crazy” and “a ridiculous amount of money,” especially for a property that would need to be rezoned before a school could be built.

“It’s a massive risk,” the source said, noting that Abbotsford has historically been reluctant to tweak its Official Community Plan to accommodate new uses within established zones.

Similarly, the province paid several times Farm Credit Canada’s reported regional average of $104,600 for agricultural parcels last year to acquire the farmland for the new Plant and Animal Health Centre. With farmland values in B.C. declining over the past 18 months, the province’s premium looks even more egregious.

While the purchase price was “well below” the prices of nearby retail or industrial properties, the site was purchased as actively farmed land within the Agricultural Land Reserve that would require a non-farm use application.

“Why the province paid so dearly for it, relative to what Panatch paid in 2020, is a bit of a mystery,” said Paul Richter, director of market analytics with CoStar. “They did go through the process to get ALC approval to subdivide into two parcels, and for ‘non-farm use’ approvals to permit the [Plant and Animal Health] Centre. This could have added value, for the right buyer. In this case, the only buyer that would have likely stepped up, stepped up. The province.”

The spending practices of other levels of government offer a point of comparison for the province’s land acquisitions.

The Department of National Defence acquired two multi-family properties on Vancouver Island last year to house personnel. A newly built 37-unit property at 244 Island Highway in View Royal traded in early October 2025 for $23.4 million, or an average of $631,622 per door unit—the most expensive multi-family transaction in Greater Victoria last year, according to CBRE Ltd. statistics.

Near CFB Comox, DND bought a 52-unit property at 574 Cumberland Rd., Courtenay, from Simba Investments Ltd. for $19.1 million. The purchase price averaged $367,308 a door—a premium versus the Mid-Island average at mid-year as reported by CBRE of $200,938 per door.

Within the Lower Mainland, the City of Coquitlam paid $3 million—or an average of $16.7 million per acre—in August 2025 for a 0.18-acre medium-density residential development site at 570 Austin Ave., Coquitlam.

The various government transactions, all completed within a few months of one another and involving different asset types, show a willingness to spend well beyond what the private sector would pay.

“It’s definitely a trend,” said the industry source familiar with the history of the Pratt Road site. “With half the developers I have done business with over the years, it’s well known that if they’re moving forward with a property, it’s because they’ve done their due diligence and they know that they can make money doing this. And they do that because they’re responsible for their own private capital and don’t want to lose money.”

items.title: Global mobility’s compliance blind spots are costing organizations
items.description: As cross-border work normalizes, employers face a mounting immigration, tax, and reputational exposure without adequate governance in place
items.content: <p>As cross-border work normalizes, employers face a mounting immigration, tax, and reputational exposure without adequate governance in place</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/036/0287_639281217985765444.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: As cross-border work normalizes, employers face a mounting immigration, tax, and reputational exposure without adequate governance in place
items.body:
The way Canadian organizations manage their people’s movement across borders has changed fundamentally – and most HR teams haven’t kept pace. As cross-border work shifts from structured international assignments to informal arrangements involving remote work, frequent business travel, and digital nomad arrangements, compliance obligations have multiplied without a corresponding evolution in governance.

The risks are unlike anything the industry has previously navigated, says Jack Kim, Partner in the Toronto office of Fragomen, a global immigration services firm. “The global mobility environment is quite in flux and you have a lot of tensions grappling against each other,” says Kim. He says that demand for global talent is surging in priority sectors including defence, energy, and infrastructure, but political headwinds at home and abroad are complicating access to that talent as enforcement tightens worldwide.

The data underscores the problem. According to global workforce management firm ECA’s Global Mobility Now 2026 study, two-thirds of global employers have no formal process for reviewing compliance implications, such as immigration limits or internal company thresholds. With nearly half of organizations in the study expecting business travel to increase and international remote work to grow over the next two years, that gap is only widening.

When informal mobility becomes a liability

Compliance problems rarely begin with a policy failure, says Kim. More often, they start with a routine trip. An employee travels repeatedly to a client in the U.S. A specialist is dispatched to an overseas facility under no formal assignment structure. None of these situations looks like a traditional global mobility file – but each can trigger payroll obligations, immigration requirements and corporate tax exposure simultaneously, he says.

“Especially on the tax front, it’s a pain in the butt to track where are my employees on any given day,” Kim says, noting that technology helps but there are also cultural questions to be considered. “And that has increased the need for employers to be able to do exactly what governments are trying to do. Where is a person on any given day? Are there a certain number of days that trigger a tax complication or an immigration complication as well? And then how do I do it?”

When individual non-compliance goes undetected, the consequences rarely stay contained. Kim points to a recent U.S. enforcement action at a battery plant in Atlanta involving a Korean company, as a cautionary example of how quickly a workforce issue becomes a geopolitical one. “Hundreds of people were apprehended at the same time, and it caused lots of news stories and consternation from governments,” he says. “It turned into a bilateral issue and a geopolitical issue.”

Kim cautions Canadian organizations against treating such scenarios as distinctly American. “This could also happen in different countries as well because the number one question, especially in countries that are facing populist-type movements, is that they don’t want people to be working illegally inside their country, and no political party wants to own that as part of a scandal.”

The case for centralized mobility governance

The decentralized approach many organizations default to – leaving individual entities or regional HR teams to manage their own immigration processes independently – is no longer adequate. Leaving immigration or compliance processes siloed across business units or provinces is a structural liability at this stage of regulatory complexity, according to Kim. “Those days are probably over because of all the complexities that you have to think about, and the dependencies between everything that happens,” he says.

Greater visibility at the executive level is equally important. Kim uses the example of a travel ban enacted by Canada during a public health emergency in Africa from Ebola to illustrate how a mobility gap becomes a leadership crisis overnight. “If you don’t know where your people are, and if you have a facility in the Democratic Republic of Congo, then you need to know who’s there right now visiting, and that immediately becomes a C-suite issue, whether you like it or not.”

The model Kim advocates is cross-functional by design, integrating immigration, tax, travel management, technology and HR business partners into a unified framework. Organizations building cross-border workforce compliance frameworks that address immigration, tax, and travel risk, as well as balance global hiring with cross-border compliance obligations, are better placed to manage the dependencies that determine whether international moves succeed or stall, he says.

“Those things should be thought of at the front end of decision-making, not at the back end,” Kim says. “Be proactive about these things, increasing visibility within your own companies, having policies in place and game planning, crisis control – because more often than not, as we've seen with the wars going on in the Middle East and in Ukraine, there's some more strategic planning that needs to be done and you cannot be reactive anymore.”

Canada’s regulatory reset and what it means for HR

Canada’s immigration system is itself in transition. Tighter temporary resident targets and the pending transfer of International Mobility Program (IMP) compliance oversight from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) signal a more enforcement-focused posture from Ottawa for employers navigating the process of hiring foreign workers.

Kim describes the recalibration that began in 2024 as “in spirit necessary” – a response to documented system fraud, housing shortages, and strained school capacity. But he warns that the recalibration must be carefully managed. “What we need to do as a country going forward is to think of things in a much more intentional and calculated manner, strategic,” he says.

He points to a recent government initiative prioritizing permanent residence pathways for high-wage workers as a constructive signal, but stresses that Canada’s capacity needs make continued access to international talent non-negotiable. “We want to build submarines, but we’re contracting a foreign company to build them for us for the next 30 years,” he says. “If we want to build pipelines, then we need people to help us build those because the talent doesn’t all reside in Canada.”

With below-replacement birth rates now recorded across 37 of 38 Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries according to the OECD’s Pensions at a Glance 2025 report, the competition for skilled talent will only intensify. HR leaders monitoring Canada’s evolving immigration policy landscape and its impact on workforce strategy should treat government engagement – through their own C-suite or government relations functions – as a core part of their long-term planning, according to Kim.

“We’re going to be competing for the same people across the world for years to come,” he says.

Duty of care in a volatile world

As geopolitical risk becomes a standard feature of the global operating environment, duty of care for internationally mobile employees has shifted from a compliance consideration to a strategic imperative. Kim, who was involved in emergency evacuation efforts during the Taliban’s seizure of Kabul in 2021, knows precisely what inadequate planning looks like. “That was a real frantic couple of weeks when we were trying to get people out of the country,” he says.

Knowing where employees are, what travel authorizations they hold, and where they can be safely relocated is foundational. Organizations can plan for global immigration and labour mobility trends in advance – mapping visa-free travel options, identifying jurisdictions where an entity can provide temporary shelter and defining what a safe relocation pathway looks like before a crisis demands one. HR teams developing proactive duty-of-care and crisis response programs for internationally mobile employees are increasingly setting the standard expected by both regulators and the workforce itself.

As enforcement intensifies globally – such as stricter border rules that could impact business travellers – Kim says the penalties for non-compliance will follow. “Companies are more in the crosshairs too,” he says, pointing to major corporations in the U.S. that have faced restrictions on sponsoring foreign workers following fraud-related allegations. The reputational damage, he notes, arrives well before any verdict.

“Whether those allegations have been proven or not is a different thing, but once you’re in the headlines, you’re in the headlines,” says Kim. “And so these things will likely be used more at a higher level to cut things off at the pass.”

items.title: Ottawa is selling homes fast – but building the wrong kind
items.description: A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa
items.content: <p>A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281937065157840.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A record sales run is raising questions about what gets built next in Ottawa
items.body:
Ottawa’s new home market posted its strongest September in recent memory, with 521 sales recorded. That's an 81.5% increase from the 287 transactions closed in September 2025, according to data from the Greater Ottawa Home Builders’ Association (GOHBA) and PMA Brethour Realty Group.

Month-over-month, activity climbed 12.3% from August’s 464 units. Year-to-date, 4,078 new homes have sold in Ottawa through September, up 53.8% from 2,652 at the same point last year.

Supply gap persists despite record sales pace

Housing starts in Ottawa are up 14% in 2026, with 8,169 homes under construction compared with 7,168 in the same period last year, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

However, the gains have not kept pace with demand for ownership housing. Much of that pipeline is weighted toward rental, raising the prospect that Ottawa’s affordability recovery could go into reverse if the ownership supply gap continues to widen.

Jason Burggraaf, Executive Director of the Greater Ottawa Home Builders’ Association in Ontario, said September’s gains carry an important caveat.

“September’s sales are encouraging, but CMHC’s latest report shows Ottawa still faces a widening housing supply gap, with much of its construction activity concentrated in rentals,” Burggraaf said.

“Improving affordability means supporting more ownership housing too. Finalizing the development charge reduction agreement is an immediate opportunity to lower building costs, and we’re pushing for a timely resolution so some 2026 construction can benefit.”

The concern echoes comments Burggraaf made on Ottawa’s August new home sales results, when he cautioned, “Governments need to ensure that the way we fund growth doesn’t add costs that put those homes further out of reach.”

Geographically, Ottawa’s west end captured 43% of September sales, with the south at 40%, together accounting for 83% of all transactions.

The east recorded 15% and Central Ottawa 2%. Townhomes led all product types at 44%, followed by single-detached homes at 35% and condo townhomes at 20%.

Development charge relief within reach

City council approved a plan in July to reduce development charges by 54% over three years, tied to a joint federal-Ontario infrastructure fund.

Under that framework, charges on single-family and semi-detached homes inside the Greenbelt would fall to $25,752, with suburban builds set at $28,781.

Development charges are one-time fees levied on new residential properties to fund growth-related capital infrastructure.

The push to finalise the agreement comes as Canada’s housing affordability reached a four-year best in Q1 2026, according to RBC Economics, with the national aggregate measure falling to 53% of pre-tax median household income required to cover ownership costs.

items.title: Canadian consumer confidence climbs, but housing optimism lags
items.description: Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision
items.content: <p>Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639281927714349803.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Home price optimism trails as brokers brace for the Bank of Canada’s October 28 decision
items.body:
Canadian consumer confidence firmed in mid-October, yet Canadians’ outlook for home values, the measure that matters most to mortgage brokers, still sits well below its historical norm.

The Bloomberg Nanos Canadian Confidence Index (BNCCI) reached 51.68 for the four weeks ending October 16, up from 49.86 a month earlier.

The weekly gauge is compiled from a rolling telephone survey of 1,016 Canadians. It sits above the neutral 50 mark but below its long-run average of 54.66 since 2008.

Almost all of the improvement came from the forward-looking side of the survey.

"The improvement was driven largely by brighter expectations: that sub-index climbed to 48.41 from 44.82. Pocketbook confidence, covering personal finances and job security, was broadly unchanged at 54.94," said Nik Nanos, chief data scientist at Nanos Research.

"Even so, overall confidence remains below its long-run average of 54.66, suggesting Canadians are feeling somewhat better, but remain cautious about the economic outlook as the year moves ahead."

What do Canadians expect from home prices?

The Expectations Index combines views on the economy with views on neighbourhood real estate, and the housing component remains soft.

Just 29.10% of respondents expect local home values to rise over the next six months. That is below the 2026 average of 34.28% and the long-run average of 39.76%.

Another 45.65% expect prices to hold, while 19.96% anticipate a decline.

Household finances offer little cushion. Only 11.03% said their personal finances improved over the past year, compared with 37.91% who said they were worse off.

British Columbia was the only region in net-negative territory, at 46.02. Ontario sat just under neutral at 49.91.

A new international research by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) revealed that Canada’s inflation-adjusted home prices more than doubled between 2005 and 2025, rising 101% and outpacing every major peer country.

Fausto Gaudio of IC Savings argues that home prices remain too disconnected from incomes, making it increasingly difficult for first-time buyers to enter the market and highlighting the need for a broader affordability reset. https://t.co/3PehdHgrJn — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 13, 2026

How the confidence data fits the Bank of Canada rate call

Nanos said the Expectations Index has tracked year-over-year GDP growth with a 0.82 correlation on a six-month lag, and that the data has been cited in the Bank of Canada’s Monetary Policy Report. That makes the reading a timely input one week before the central bank’s October 28 decision. The overnight rate has stood at 2.25% since October 2025.

Most of the bank economists calling for an October 28 rate hold point to September’s inflation data.

Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres Group, addressed those figures amid rising business inflation expectations in the Bank’s latest survey.

“The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting,” she said.

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada in Montréal, has urged brokers to recommend the five-year fixed over variable. He was direct about the risk of tightening. 

“I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive,” he noted.

items.title: Feeling Creative? Good Bones Hit The Trinity Bellwoods Market
items.description:
Our typical listing spotlight features the standard bells and whistles, including savvy staging. But sometimes, all it takes to make the eyes (and heart) linger is a bare-bones set of photos and a strong foundation.

This is the case with 13 Euclid Avenue. Tucked north of Queen, just around the corner from Trinity Bellwoods Park, this duplex — asking $999,700 — hits the market with its upper levels presenting as a clean state. With no staging, renderings, or AI imaginings (phew), the home can’t hide.

But with quality craftsmanship, that's not a problem.

Across 2.5 storeys, multiple elements feel (and may just be) straight from a past era. On arrival, you’re met by original hardwood flooring, which continues to make appearances across other areas of the home (including the top-floor bedroom — more on that shortly).

Original millwork, detailed plaster ceilings that soar to generous heights, and large windows that fill the space with natural light all bring a special type of character that’s difficult to emulate in a new build.

  • SPECS

    • Address: 13 Euclid Avenue, Toronto
    • Bedrooms: 4
    • Bathrooms: 2
    • Size: 1,500-2,000 sq. ft
    • Listed At: $999,700

The address is a working duplex; the lower unit — complete with its own kitchen and walkout to the backyard — is home to a tenant who, according to the listing, is happy to stay in place.

Make no mistake: there’s room for renovation and upgrades here, too. Whether it’s transforming the upper kitchen into an eat-in paradise, or combining landscaping with outdoor furniture to create a private backyard sanctuary, your imagination is the limit. But please, buyer-to-be — leave the blue bathroom tile intact.

______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Our Favourite Thing

We've already given the bathroom tile its flowers, so here we'll celebrate the main top-level bedroom. Spanning some half of the home's top floor, this room features hardwood planks that are wider than elsewhere in the home — and we're swooning over them. Pair that floor with the uniquely angular ceiling, a skylight, and the quirky shelf built into the wall, and you have the perfect place to design a primary-bedroom sanctuary. That, or a reading nook for the ages.

______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

This address also comes complete with a detached garage off the laneway, a rare find for the area.

And speaking of the neighbourhood: beyond the craftsmanship, a key part of this home’s charm is its location — literal steps from the Queen West strip, calling 13 Euclid home would mean coffee at White Squirrel followed by a walk in the park as a daily routine. Sud Forno sandwiches would probably beckon most days, too. But we wouldn’t mind.

items.title: Empty homes tax debate swirls 10 years after pioneering tax in Vancouver
items.description: Developers warn the empty homes tax could increase costs and undermine new construction
items._ogDesc: Developers warn the empty homes tax could increase costs and undermine new construction
items.body:
The City of Vancouver launched a tax on empty dwellings 10 years ago that it billed as the first municipal tax of its kind anywhere in North America.

Debate swirls around how effective taxing empty homes is in helping the long-term housing market. This is despite even critics accepting that these taxes can help reduce the number of empty dwellings.

Since Vancouver introduced that initial empty homes tax, the concept has proved popular in public polling and among left-of-centre politicians that created similar themed taxes at the provincial and federal levels.

Governments roll out empty homes taxes over past decade

Gregor Robertson was Vancouver's mayor when he and his Vision Vancouver council approved the city's Empty Homes Tax (EHT) in November 2016. This came into effect Jan. 1, 2017.

Vancouver homeowners must submit an annual declaration so the city can determine whether their property is subject to the EHT.

Properties deemed or declared empty in 2025, for example, are subject to a three per cent tax on the property’s 2025 assessed value.

Former premier John Horgan and his NDP government were next to launch a tax on those who own vacant dwellings.

Enacted in 2018, the province's Speculation and Vacancy Tax (SVT) had its first declaration period for property owners in January and February 2019.

The SVT applies to municipalities across Metro Vancouver, the Capital Regional District in Greater Victoria and 26 other municipalities.

The province slaps a one per cent annual tax on Canadian citizens and permanent residents who own homes they leave vacant, while foreign residents who do that get a bigger tax bill, equal to three per cent of their property's assessed taxable value.

Former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's government introduced its Underused Housing Tax (UHT) to take effect in January 2022.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government then earlier this year cancelled the UHT, saying the tax was costly and inefficient to administer, generating excessive compliance burdens and red tape for taxpayers.

Politicians promise new taxes on empty dwellings

Recent provincial and municipal election campaigns have provided further evidence of the popularity of the empty homes tax, particularly among left-of-centre politicians.

Former NDP MLA and Imagine Surrey leader Mike Starchuk, for example, promised during his recent failed mayoral campaign he would call on the provincial government to amend its Local Government Act to allow the City of Surrey create its own empty homes tax.

Vancouver was legally able to launch its pioneering EHT because it is governed by the Vancouver charter, which allows special taxing powers.

In contrast, the Local Government Act and Community Charter, which govern Surrey and other cities across the province, do not allow the same taxing powers.

Starchuk said he would apply his proposed municipal empty homes tax on dwellings left vacant for much of the year.

His intent is to reduce the asking price for new rents and help people find homes.

Starchuk said the initiative would also generate revenue to help fund affordable housing projects.

He is not alone in wanting to use taxation to help free up potential homes.

B.C. Premier David Eby, as NDP leader during the current election campaign, promised two separate measures to tax empty homes.

First, he pledged to introduce a new tax on condominiums that developers have completed but not sold.

This new condo tax would apply to finished units that have been left empty for more than a year and start at a two per cent rate.

The tax rate would then rise by one percentage point for each additional year that the units remain unsold and unoccupied, Eby said.

Eby explained the proposal in part by pointing to a Real Property Data report showing developers are sitting on about $4.4 billion worth of completed but empty homes.

Eby separately promised to increase the SVT’s rates to two per cent for domestic owners and to five per cent for foreign owners.

Number of empty homes fall in Vancouver after tax introduced

Reaction to the general concept of empty homes tax is mixed. Supporters point out evidence that the tax reduces the number of vacant homes. Others warn of unintended consequences and potential long-term harm to the housing market and economy.

Geoff Meggs, a Vision Vancouver councillor in the mid-2010s, told Business in Vancouver that he originally opposed the idea of bringing in an empty homes tax in Vancouver.

Vision Vancouver pushed for an empty homes tax while he was in office.

"I had reservations because it was not clear to me how big a problem it actually was," Meggs said.

Urban planning consultant Andy Yan had conducted a study of empty condominiums that used various data, including electricity consumption, to determine that Vancouver had a substantial number of vacant units.

Yan told BIV that his research focused on specific neighbourhoods in downtown Vancouver.

"The public was concerned because there were not enough lights on," Meggs said.

"But I wasn't sure how you could be sure that a place was empty, and therefore taxable. And how would you enforce it? I had all these questions, but we decided to do it because there was a lot of public concern."

He said his reticence turned out to be unfounded.

"The city was able to set up a system where people were required to disclose," he said. "It was quite simple. People had thought it would take forms that would go on forever, but it was a very straightforward online process that people declared and then people had to pay the tax."

Since the city implemented the tax, its data has shown a steady decline in the percentage of vacant homes in the city.

The city's annual report on the tax released last year showed, based on homeowner declarations, just 0.49 per cent of the homes in Vancouver are vacant—the lowest percentage since the tax launched.

That figure excludes vacant homes exempt from the tax because of fire damage, a court order restricting their use, a recent death or other reasons that the city considers valid.

The city's vacant home rate was 1.17 per cent in 2017, and in each successive year showed a decline.

In total, the number of vacant and exempted homes in Vancouver in 2024 was 4,697, or about 2.3 per cent of the city’s 201,739 total homes.

Of the other homes, 136,211 are principal residences and 60,831 are tenanted, according to the city.

Yan said he believes targeted taxes are effective at reducing the number of empty homes.

He pointed to a 2022 report by UBC economists Tsur Somerville and Jake Wetzel that found B.C.'s SVT has also been successful, returning approximately 20,000 vacant housing units to the long-term rental market in Metro Vancouver.

Taxes come with unintended consequences

Developers say taxes on vacant homes or on unsold inventory are misguided because they increase the cost of future development and can make projects financially unviable.

When developers get financing, they document their costs and risks and bring that to bankers, explained Michael Geller, a principal at Michael Geller Associates Ltd. and a longtime developer of small projects.

Higher costs and the risk of future taxes can force developers to take out larger loans and, in some cases, borrow at higher interest rates, he said.

One of Geller's main objections is that Vancouver's EHT is charged not only on empty homes, but also on empty development sites.

The city's rationale is that homeowners should not be able to avoid the tax by demolishing their dwellings, he explained.

The problem is that a development site can remain untouched because it is not financially viable for the owner to build homes and sell them at prices that cover costs and generate a profit, Geller said.

"The developer's permits may be held up," he added. "Maybe he can't arrange financing because there is no market. Meanwhile, in addition to his property taxes, he's now paying this empty homes tax that, one day, he'll have to try to recover from developing homes."

Geller also opposes Eby's promise to tax developers' unsold inventory of homes that have been vacant for more than a year.

Eby said at a news conference that B.C. needs this tax because developers are "hoarding" those units, waiting for them to go up in price.

"Nothing could be further from the truth," Geller told BIV. "The notion that they're hoarding them and keeping them off the market to maybe make them more valuable is preposterous."

The reality, he explained, is that lenders restrict developers' ability to sell the units.

Bankers almost always have clauses in lending agreements that set minimum prices at which developers are allowed to can sell units, he said.

If a developer sells a unit for below that set price, then the banker would require the developer to put in more capital of his or her own, Geller said.

He said bankers put these kinds of clauses in projects he developed, such as:

  • the four-unit Vinson House in West Vancouver;
  • the four-unit Ambleside Mews in West Vancouver; and
  • the 36-unit Elm Park Place in Vancouver.

Other developers stressed that developers are selling units as fast as they can.

Polygon Homes chairman Michael Audain told BIV that taxing empty homes or unsold condos is the "craziest idea I've ever heard."

He stressed that every completed condo that his company builds, it tries to sell as soon as it can. 

"We're not selling, certainly, at the rate that we were a few years ago, but we're selling everywhere at whatever the market will allow us to do because that's our business—to build and sell homes," he said. 

"There's no point putting a hammer on the developer to sell. The absorption can only be at a certain level, and demand is very low at the moment. You can't dump all your homes on the market at once."

Other developers told BIV that taxing developers for unsold inventory makes future development more costly, if not impossible.

"If the government is at all interested in encouraging housing development, this basically just shuts it down," Cressey Development Group executive vice-president Hani Lammam told BIV.

He said Cressey has no unsold inventory, although that could change this spring.

That is when Cressey expects to complete its 59-unit Rockford condominium project in Surrey, where 43 units were pre-sold.

Lammam said governments brought in empty homes taxes partly in response to the perception that wealthy foreign buyers owned B.C. homes as secondary residences.

"Circumstances have changed," Lammam said.

"There are no investors, virtually whatsoever, in the marketplace. The cost to produce the housing, when you aggregate all costs, is unaffordable for local incomes. So, the whole model is broken. Costs have to come down, or incomes have to go up."

Cressey has shifted over the past decade toward building more rental buildings and fewer condominium developments.

A tax on unsold inventory might push other developers to similarly shift toward building rental homes, Lammam said.

But he cautioned that building rental housing today is also challenging.

"Building rental was viable," he said. "Is it viable today, and are we starting new rental projects today? No, we're not because the costs are high and revenues are weak, and there's a flood of inventory."

That oversupply includes a major project by the Squamish First Nation, which has been able to build using different development requirements because the projects are on Squamish territory, he said.

The Squamish First Nation has finished the first phase of its Sen̓áḵw project at the south end of the Burrard Bridge—a development that has far less parking than the City of Vancouver would otherwise require.

That first phase delivered 1,409 units across three towers. When complete, Sen̓áḵw is expected to be the largest rental project in Vancouver's history, with 11 residential towers delivering providing more than 6,000 purpose-built rental homes.

The Musqueam First Nation is involved in East Wind near UBC which is expected to deliver 451 rental homes, including apartments and townhouses, by 2029.

items.body:
Is it a bird? A plane? No, it’s… the size of Canada’s debt servicing costs. The Parliamentary Budget Officer’s (PBO) latest Economic and Fiscal Outlook projects Ottawa will accumulate $333 billion in deficit spending over 5 years. However, the Government of Canada (GoC) will need to borrow nearly three-quarters of a trillion dollars. Debt servicing is now the fastest-growing federal expense, projected to consume almost 1 in 7 dollars of revenue by 2030.

Federal Borrowing To Grow More Than 2x As Much As Deficits

Ottawa will accumulate $333.3 billion in cumulative deficits from 2026-27 through 2030-31. At the same time, the GoC will borrow an additional $732.9 billion, according to the PBO’s projections. That’s roughly 2.2 times as much borrowing than the projected deficit—or a deficit less than half the size of new borrowing. It depends on whether you’re a half-insolvent or half-solvent kind of person.

One of the reasons behind the gap is accounting methodology. Loans are both a liability and an asset; just think of it like a mortgage. One borrower’s liability of $100k is an asset of $100k to the lender. In this case, the gap is driven by Crown corporations and acquiring other assets. When the GoC borrows $1 billion and lends it to a Crown corporation, it owes investors $1 billion, but it’s also owed $1 billion. The loan doesn’t increase the deficit, just interest costs and any resulting losses.

It’s debatable whether it’s a good or bad decision, but the consequences are much clearer. “Most simply, cash outlays drive borrowing, which in turn increase market debt and public debt charges, independent of how they are recorded on an accrual basis,” warns the PBO.

The PBO’s calculations show a sharp impact on public finances in the coming years.

Canada To Spend Almost 1 In 7 Dollars of Revenue On Debt Payments

The PBO warns that debt charges are now the fastest-growing public expense. Annual public debt charges are projected to climb from $24.5 billion in 2021-22 to $59.3 billion in 2026-27. Their projections show it explodes to $83.0 billion in 2030-31, much faster than revenue. The PBO estimates debt repayment will consume 13.6% of revenue by 2030-31, up from 10.5% in 2025-26. Debt servicing is set to grow 29.5% faster than revenue, consuming almost 1 in 7 dollars collected.

Most are likely to assume this is due to higher interest rates, but that’s not what the numbers show. The PBO explains that this mainly reflects a larger stock of debt, not higher interest rates. That’s the fanciest way to say the captain of this ship didn’t realize they lost their anchor.
